# 2023 Annual Budget Review

## Summary
I spread the twelve months of statements across the kitchen table in early January and worked through them with a pencil, because the screen makes everything look the same. My savings rate came out at 19% of take-home pay, which is short of the quarter I had hoped for but honest given how the year actually ran. Income was flat from January to December, no raise, no bonus, just the same figure landing on the last working day of each month. I paid myself first, moving a fixed sum into the savings account on the first working day, before rent or food or anything else got a look at it. That single habit did more for the year than any clever adjustment later on. There were two surprises, both on the spending side rather than the earning side, and I have written them down plainly below because pretending they did not happen would make the review useless.

Actually, the discipline of the transfer mattered more than the size of it. Some months the sum was small, some months I could push a little more across, but the money left the current account before I had a chance to form an opinion about it. I kept no separate pot for emergencies, which in hindsight was a gap, but I never had to dip into the savings either. The year felt tight in the ordinary way rather than the frightening way, and that is roughly what a nineteen per cent rate buys you when nothing dramatic goes wrong.

## Expenses
Rent took 32% of income, the largest single line by a wide margin and the one I watch hardest each month. Groceries averaged 380 EUR a month, a touch under the 400 EUR I had pencilled in, because I did one deliberate shop a week instead of drifting through the shop three or four times. I kept a rough tally on the fridge door and it kept me honest. The holiday fund was the big one: I had set aside 900 EUR for a week in the Lakes, and that is exactly what the week cost, trains, cottage and all the meals out included. It was the only proper break of the year and I do not regret a euro of it. Then the unexpected arrived in September, 600 EUR for a bike after the frame on the old one cracked at the bottom bracket, which no spreadsheet could have seen coming. Utilities ran close to plan through the winter, though the electric was heavier than I expected in the cold snap. Insurance and the phone bill both stayed flat. Subscriptions added up to more than I would have guessed, small amounts that never feel like real money until they are totalled at the end of the year. The bike is the single line I would defend hardest, since it replaced the commuting machine I use four days a week. Looking back, those two shocks together came to well over a tenth of the year's spending, and neither was avoidable in any way I can see. I have stopped treating a year like that as a failure.

## Next Year
For next year I want the savings rate to move up rather than sideways, so the first change is a slightly larger transfer on the first working day, even if it means a leaner month here and there. Rent is the lever I cannot pull much, so I will leave that alone unless the lease gives me room. Groceries get a firm 400 EUR ceiling and a running total I actually check. I will start a small separate pot for the things that break, so the next cracked frame does not land on the year as a shock. And I want one proper week away again, budgeted in advance rather than improvised. If the income finally moves, I will put half the rise straight into savings rather than letting it drift into everyday spending, since that has been the leak each year. Insurance renewals get checked rather than accepted, and I want to stop buying coffee out on weekday mornings, which added up to more than I would like across twelve months.
